title: Trump Claims He Gave Fed Chair Warsh 'Permission' to Hike Rates, Igniting Independence Debate
snippet: President Donald Trump raised eyebrows by suggesting Fed Chair Kevin Warsh consulted him before a key interest rate decision, stoking fresh concerns over the central bank's political independence.
content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has stirred up new questions regarding the Federal Reserve's political independence after suggesting he gave central bank Chair Kevin Warsh implicit authorization to proceed with a recent interest rate hike.

Speaking to reporters following the Fed's first rate increase in three years, Trump claimed he advised Warsh—his own nominee—to vote with the central bank's rate-setting board because the Fed chair was simply outnumbered by a "hostile" committee.

"I talked to Kevin and I said you might as well vote with the board because it’s not going to matter… I said, ‘Do what you want because it doesn’t matter’ because he doesn’t have the votes," Trump said, implying the move was incorrect but unavoidable.

Concerns Over Central Bank Autonomy

The president's comments immediately drew skepticism and concern from Wall Street analysts and former Federal Reserve officials. The central bank is intentionally structured to operate independently from executive politics, ensuring monetary policy decisions are driven by long-term economic data rather than short-term political pressures.

"It’s an unusual and unfortunate comment to make. Clearly, the Fed chair does not need the president’s permission to raise rates," said Eric Rosengren, former president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston. "The implication is that the chair got a hall pass."

Krishna Guha, vice chairman at Evercore ISI, pushed back on the idea that Warsh was pressured or required presidential approval. "The market believes—and with good grounds—that Kevin Warsh owned this decision and that the committee was strongly united behind him," Guha noted, stressing there was no indication Warsh was coerced into the policy shift.

Staying in Their Lanes

When asked directly at a news conference about his recent communications with the White House, Warsh declined to detail private conversations, choosing instead to emphasize institutional boundaries.

"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane. Independence is a two-way street," Warsh said. "We’ll let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane, too."

Economic policy experts warn that even the perception of executive interference could shake financial markets. If investors come to believe the central bank is taking cues from the administration, it could erode public confidence, unhinge inflation expectations, and ultimately drive up borrowing costs across mortgages, auto loans, and corporate debt.
